subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Georges Lemaître: The Father of the Big Bang
description: Learn Georges Lemaître: The Father of the Big Bang in one minute.

hook.text: A Belgian priest first proposed that the universe began from a 'primeval atom.' Physicists laughed at him.

buildup.text: Georges Lemaître published his idea in 1927—two years before Hubble's observations supported it.

discovery.text: He derived the expanding universe from Einstein's equations. Einstein dismissed it: 'Your physics is abominable.'

twist.text: Fred Hoyle coined 'Big Bang' as a mocking term on BBC radio in 1949. The name stuck despite the ridicule.

climax.text: Lemaître lived to see the CMB discovery in 1965, finally proving his theory correct. He died in 1966.

punchline.text: A priest proposed the Big Bang. A critic accidentally named it.

quiz.question: Who first proposed that the universe expanded from a 'primeval atom'?
options: Georges Lemaître, a Belgian priest and physicist
Edwin Hubble, based on galaxy observations
Albert Einstein, from his theory of general relativity

details.summary: Georges Lemaître, a Belgian priest and physicist, first proposed in 1927 that the universe is expanding and originated from a 'primeval atom' — the earliest version of the Big Bang theory.
details.whyItMatters: Lemaître deserves recognition as the true originator of the Big Bang theory and the expanding universe concept. His work shows how scientific credit can be lost through language barriers and institutional biases.
takeaways: Lemaître proposed the expanding universe and Big Bang in 1927
He derived Hubble's Law two years before Hubble published it
His work was initially overlooked due to language barriers

faq.question: Why isn't Hubble's Law called Lemaître's Law?
faq.answer: In 2018, the International Astronomical Union officially renamed it the Hubble-Lemaître Law, acknowledging Lemaître's prior discovery. For decades, Hubble received sole credit because Lemaître's 1927 paper was in French.

faq.question: Was there conflict between Lemaître's science and his faith?
faq.answer: Lemaître kept them strictly separate. When Pope Pius XII proclaimed the Big Bang as proof of creation, Lemaître strongly objected, insisting his theory was scientific, not theological. He believed science and faith operated in different domains and neither should be used to justify the other.
